title: Across 90 OpenNeuro studies with brief task events, regions with a later resting BOLD lag have later and longer event responses; the pattern held in 43 held-out studies
abstract:
Brain regions whose slow spontaneous BOLD signal arrives late at rest also have later and longer responses to brief task events. A resting delay map from other people therefore predicts a modest but consistent part of the regional timing of task fMRI responses, which analyses that assume one response timing for all regions ignore.

We used ReadyNeuro, minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro fMRI without slice-timing correction. For 115 study-tasks in 90 studies (702 people, about 105 task labels), we estimated the group event response of 226 regions with a finite impulse response (FIR) model. Latency is the time shift that aligns a region's whole response curve with the study's dominant response. We compared it with a resting lag map from 80 other studies (138 people): the delay of each region's slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) spontaneous signal behind the cortical mean.

In 47 discovery studies, the median per-study Spearman correlation was 0.33 (45 of 47 positive), and latency increased by 0.49 s per 1 s of resting lag. We then registered eight tests. In 43 confirmation studies, the correlation was 0.43 (39 of 43 positive, p = 4e-8), the slope was 0.50 (95% CI 0.41-0.58), and the discovery latency map predicted each new study (median 0.58). The correlations exceeded all 1,000 surrogate maps with the same spatial smoothness. Post hoc, per 1 s of resting lag the response rose 0.2-0.3 s later, peaked 0.4 s later and ended 0.6 s later, so late regions respond later and longer. The relation held in grey matter only, for deactivating regions, and after control for predicted slice-acquisition time and temporal signal-to-noise ratio. Thalamus, ventral diencephalon and brainstem responded 0.2-0.5 s earlier than the map predicts; putamen and cerebellum responded later. The pre-registered slice-timing positive control failed, because one study gives slice times in milliseconds; post hoc, without that study, the control was positive (slope -0.67; expected -1).

Limits: coarse atlas regions after rigid alignment, 8 people per study, one response shape per run, and no physiological recordings.
